triage.name: Diabetes Type 2
triage.reason: Very common clinic presentation with subtle symptoms, screening labs and a broad complication differential; strong teaching case.

review_issues: labs k: both high and low across severities

demographics: More common in Black, Hispanic/Latino, American Indian, Asian American, and Pacific Islander adults in the US
Slightly more common in men in middle age; more common in women at older ages
Increasingly diagnosed in adolescents and young adults, especially with obesity

risk_factors.text: History of gestational diabetes or a baby weighing 9 pounds or more at birth
High blood pressure or high triglycerides with low HDL cholesterol
Acanthosis nigricans (dark velvety skin at the neck or armpits)
Chronic use of glucocorticoids or atypical antipsychotics

family_history: Type 2 diabetes in a parent or sibling
social_history: Sedentary work or little regular exercise
Diets high in refined carbohydrates and sugar-sweetened drinks
Limited access to healthy food or preventive care

chief_complaints.text: I'm up all night going to the bathroom
I just feel tired all the time
My doctor said my sugar was high on my blood work
I've lost some weight without trying
The sore on my foot just won't heal

hpi.onset: Gradual, often over months to years; many patients cannot name when it started
hpi.duration: Symptoms usually present for months; a third or more of patients have no symptoms and are found on routine labs
hpi.progression: Slowly worsening thirst, urination and fatigue; symptoms may be mild enough to ignore until a routine visit or a complication brings them in
hpi.location: Whole-body; foot numbness or tingling is in the feet and hands
hpi.quality: Thirst is constant and hard to satisfy; urination is frequent, including at night; fatigue is a heavy, low-energy feeling
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; patients often say they thought it was just getting older
hpi.timing: Thirst and urination are worse at night and after meals; fatigue is worse in the afternoon
relieving: Drinking water briefly helps the thirst
Rest helps the tiredness a little

associated_symptoms.text: Frequent urination, including waking at night
Blurred vision that comes and goes
Numbness, tingling or burning in the feet

pertinent_negatives: Vomiting and deep rapid breathing (as in diabetic ketoacidosis)
Sudden severe weight loss over weeks
One-sided weakness, numbness or trouble speaking
Symptoms that began over days rather than months

positives.text: Numbness or tingling in the feet
Burning pain in the feet at night
Dark velvety skin at the neck or armpits

atypical.how_it_differs: Type 2 diabetes in children and teens usually comes with obesity and a strong family history; they may have no symptoms and be found on screening, or present with acanthosis nigricans and high blood pressure.
Symptoms are often blamed on aging; thirst may be blunted, and they may present with confusion, falls, poor wound healing or a hyperglycemic emergency instead of classic thirst and urination.
High blood sugar first found in pregnancy is usually gestational diabetes; it is often silent and picked up on routine screening, and it raises the risk of later type 2 diabetes.
Patients with obesity may have insulin resistance and acanthosis nigricans for years before glucose rises; symptoms stay mild and the diagnosis is often made on screening labs.

general.mild: Well-appearing, often overweight or obese, no distress
general.moderate: Well-appearing but tired; may look overweight with central adiposity
general.critical: Lethargic or obtunded, dry mucous membranes, deep rapid breathing, signs of shock

findings.maneuver: Measure height and weight and calculate BMI; measure waist circumference
findings.finding: BMI in the overweight or obese range with central adiposity

findings.maneuver: Inspect the back of the neck, axillae and skin folds
findings.finding: Dark, thick, velvety skin in flexural areas
Small skin tags

findings.maneuver: Inspect the soles, between the toes and over pressure points of both feet
findings.finding: Non-healing ulcer or callus, often at a pressure point

findings.maneuver: Inspect the feet for deformity and dry, cracked skin
findings.finding: Hammer toes, prominent metatarsal heads, dry fissured skin

findings.maneuver: Palpate the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses
findings.finding: Diminished or absent pedal pulses

findings.maneuver: Test light touch and pinprick over the distal feet in a stocking distribution
findings.finding: Reduced sensation in a symmetric stocking distribution

findings.maneuver: Test vibration sense with a 128 Hz tuning fork at the great toe
findings.finding: Reduced or absent vibration sense
Absent ankle reflexes

findings.maneuver: Test with a 10 g monofilament at the plantar surface of the foot
findings.finding: Loss of protective sensation
Arteriovenous nicking, cotton wool spots or flame hemorrhages
Microaneurysms, dot-blot hemorrhages, hard exudates or neovascularization

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lens with a penlight or ophthalmoscope
findings.finding: Lens opacity

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oral mucosa and tongue
findings.finding: Dry mucous membranes

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oral cavity and tongue
findings.finding: White plaques consistent with oral thrush
Clear breath sounds without crackles or wheeze

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart and check for jugular venous distension and edema
findings.finding: No murmur, no JVD, no peripheral edema
Soft, non-tender, no organomegaly or mass

findings.maneuver: Assess orientation and level of alertness
findings.finding: Alert and oriented, normal attention

labs.caveat: Reflects average glucose over about 3 months; may be falsely low with anemia, recent transfusion, or hemoglobin variants.
Fasting value; a random value over 200 mg/dL with classic symptoms also makes the diagnosis.
Rises with diabetic kidney disease; used to compute eGFR for staging.
Rises with dehydration or kidney impairment.
Low with osmotic diuresis or insulin; high with kidney failure or certain diabetes medicines.
Low with marked hyperglycemia or diuretic use; very high with severe dehydration.
Low in ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar states; a normal value argues against significant acidosis.
Low HDL is part of the insulin-resistance pattern.
Mild elevation suggests fatty liver disease, common with type 2 diabetes.
Glucose appears in urine once the blood level exceeds the renal threshold.
Large ketones with acidosis suggest ketoacidosis rather than uncomplicated type 2 diabetes.
Suggests diabetic kidney disease; confirm with a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio.
Thyroid disease clusters with type 2 diabetes and can worsen glucose control.
Elevated when there is an active infection such as a foot ulcer or urinary infection.

findings.finding: Normal sinus rhythm
Signs of left ventricular hypertrophy from long-standing hypertension
ST depression or T-wave inversion suggesting silent ischemia
Flattened or inverted T waves
Prolonged QTc with severe electrolyte disturbance

imaging.study: Dilated retinal exam or retinal photography

imaging.preferred_when: Atypical chest symptoms in a patient at intermediate risk
Carotid bruit or prior stroke or TIA
Claudication, non-healing foot ulcer, or absent pedal pulses

findings.text: Reduced ankle-brachial index indicating peripheral arterial disease
Falsely elevated index from arterial calcification

imaging.preferred_when: Right upper quadrant pain or abnormal liver enzymes

findings.text: Increased hepatic echogenicity suggesting fatty liver

initial.why: Confirms the diagnosis and sets the baseline for control
Fasting plasma glucose is an alternative diagnostic test
Assesses kidney function, electrolytes and acid-base status
Screens for glucose, ketones and protein in the urine
Liver enzymes and albumin as part of the metabolic assessment

initial.test: Dilated retinal exam or retinal photography

initial.only_if: claudication, non-healing foot ulcer, or absent pedal pulses

supporting.why: Thyroid disease is common and can affect glucose control
Markers of inflammation track with insulin resistance
supporting.only_if: features suggest an inflammatory or infectious process
fever, foot ulcer, or urinary symptoms

not_indicated.why: No role in the evaluation of hyperglycemia
Not needed unless there is acidosis or hypoperfusion
Not part of the diabetes workup
Not routine; reserve for selected patients with chest symptoms
not_indicated.only_if: atypical chest symptoms in an intermediate-risk patient

decision_points: Confirm an abnormal screening result with a second test unless the patient has unequivocal symptoms with a glucose of 200 mg/dL or higher
Check for ketones and acidosis if the patient is vomiting, breathing deeply, or has severe hyperglycemia
Screen for retinopathy, kidney disease and neuropathy at diagnosis and then at recommended intervals
Treat cardiovascular risk factors, not just glucose

criteria.name: American Diabetes Association diagnostic thresholds
criteria.summary: Diabetes is diagnosed when any one of the following is met and confirmed: A1C of 6.5% or higher, fasting plasma glucose of 126 mg/dL or higher after at least 8 hours of fasting, a 2-hour plasma glucose of 200 mg/dL or higher during an oral glucose tolerance test, or a random plasma glucose of 200 mg/dL or higher in a patient with classic symptoms of hyperglycemia or a hyperglycemic crisis. In the absence of unequivocal symptoms, the same test should be repeated to confirm the result.
items: Fasting plasma glucose 126 mg/dL or higher
2-hour plasma glucose 200 mg/dL or higher on oral glucose tolerance testing
Random plasma glucose 200 mg/dL or higher with classic symptoms or hyperglycemic crisis

criteria.name: Prediabetes thresholds
criteria.summary: Prediabetes is present when glucose is above normal but below the diabetes cutoffs: A1C 5.7 to 6.4%, fasting plasma glucose 100 to 125 mg/dL, or a 2-hour plasma glucose of 140 to 199 mg/dL on oral glucose tolerance testing.

differential.name: Type 1 diabetes
differential.why_considered: Both cause hyperglycemia with thirst, urination and weight loss, and the distinction changes treatment completely.
differential.trigger: Younger or lean patient, rapid symptom onset over weeks, or ketones and acidosis at presentation

history: Symptoms develop over weeks rather than months to years
Weight loss is prominent despite normal or increased appetite
Personal or family history of autoimmune disease such as thyroid disease or celiac disease
exam: Often lean or normal weight rather than overweight
May appear ill or dehydrated if presenting in ketoacidosis
labs: Positive glutamic acid decarboxylase or islet antigen 2 antibodies
Low or undetectable C-peptide
Large urine ketones with a low bicarbonate and high anion gap

differential.name: Diabetic ketoacidosis
differential.why_considered: Severe hyperglycemia with dehydration, vomiting and altered mental status can be the first presentation of type 2 diabetes, especially in Black and Hispanic adults.
differential.trigger: Vomiting, deep rapid breathing, fruity breath, abdominal pain or drowsiness in a patient with very high glucose

history: Nausea and vomiting with abdominal pain
Symptoms worsening over days rather than months
Recent infection, missed medication or new steroid use
exam: Dry mucous membranes and poor skin turgor
labs: Glucose usually above 250 mg/dL
Bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L with an elevated anion gap
Moderate to large urine or serum ketones
pH below 7.30 on arterial or venous blood gas

differential.name: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
differential.why_considered: Older patients with type 2 diabetes can present with extreme hyperglycemia, profound dehydration and altered mental status without significant ketosis.
differential.trigger: Glucose often above 600 mg/dL with marked dehydration, confusion or focal neurologic deficits and minimal ketones

history: Days to weeks of worsening thirst and urination
Often triggered by infection, myocardial infarction or stroke
Lives in a nursing facility or has limited access to water
exam: Severe dehydration with dry mucous membranes and hypotension
Altered mental status ranging from confusion to coma
Focal neurologic deficits that resolve with fluid and insulin
labs: Serum osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg
Glucose often above 600 mg/dL
Bicarbonate usually above 18 mmol/L with minimal ketones
Marked prerenal azotemia with elevated BUN and creatinine

differential.name: Medication-induced hyperglycemia
differential.why_considered: Glucocorticoids, atypical antipsychotics, thiazides and calcineurin inhibitors can raise glucose and mimic new type 2 diabetes.

history: Recent start or dose increase of prednisone, olanzapine, quetiapine, hydrochlorothiazide or tacrolimus
Glucose rises after meals and in the afternoon, especially with steroids
No classic osmotic symptoms before the medication was started
labs: Hyperglycemia that improves when the offending drug is reduced or stopped
A1C may be normal if the exposure is recent

differential.name: Stress hyperglycemia
differential.why_considered: Acute illness, surgery, trauma or infection can raise glucose in patients without underlying diabetes.

history: Glucose elevated during a hospital admission for another reason
No prior history of diabetes or prediabetes
No thirst, urination or weight loss before the illness
labs: A1C in the normal range
Glucose normalizes as the acute illness resolves
Catecholamine and cortisol surge pattern with elevated glucose only during stress

differential.name: Cushing syndrome
differential.why_considered: Excess cortisol causes insulin resistance, central weight gain and hyperglycemia that can look like type 2 diabetes.

history: Progressive central weight gain with thinning arms and legs
Easy bruising, purple abdominal striae and proximal muscle weakness
Chronic glucocorticoid use is the most common cause
exam: Moon facies, buffalo hump and supraclavicular fat pads
Proximal muscle weakness on rising from a chair
labs: Elevated late-night salivary cortisol or 24-hour urine free cortisol
Failure to suppress cortisol on a low-dose dexamethasone suppression test

differential.name: Hypothyroidism
differential.why_considered: Fatigue, weight gain, dry skin and mild hyperglycemia overlap with type 2 diabetes and thyroid disease clusters with it.

history: Cold intolerance, constipation and heavy menstrual periods
Weight gain rather than weight loss
Slow speech and slowed thinking
exam: Dry coarse skin, bradycardia and delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes
labs: Elevated TSH with low free T4
Positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies if autoimmune

differential.name: Pancreatic diabetes
differential.why_considered: Chronic pancreatitis, pancreatic cancer or cystic fibrosis can destroy islet cells and cause hyperglycemia.

history: Chronic heavy alcohol use or recurrent pancreatitis
Steatorrhea with greasy, floating stools
Weight loss out of proportion to glucose elevation
exam: Epigastric tenderness or a palpable mass
labs: Low fecal elastase
Elevated lipase or amylase during flares
Low C-peptide with absent diabetes autoantibodies

differential.name: Monogenic diabetes
differential.why_considered: Maturity-onset diabetes of the young and neonatal diabetes can present with mild hyperglycemia in young, non-obese patients with a strong family history.

history: Diabetes in multiple generations with an autosomal dominant pattern
Diagnosis before age 25 in a lean patient
Mild fasting hyperglycemia that is stable for years
labs: Negative diabetes autoantibodies
Preserved C-peptide
Genetic panel identifies a specific mutation such as HNF1A or GCK

differential.name: Gestational diabetes
differential.why_considered: Hyperglycemia first recognized during pregnancy is usually gestational diabetes and is often silent.

history: Diagnosis during the second or third trimester
Prior baby weighing 9 pounds or more
Prior gestational diabetes
labs: Abnormal 50 g glucose challenge followed by an abnormal 100 g oral glucose tolerance test
A1C usually below 6.5%

severity.mild: A1C 6.5 to 7.0% on no medication or a single agent, no symptoms, no complications, normal kidney function and no albuminuria
severity.moderate: A1C 7.0 to 8.5% despite lifestyle and one or two agents, early complications such as mild retinopathy, microalbuminuria or early neuropathy, and mild hypertension
severity.severe: A1C 8.5 to 11.0% with osmotic symptoms, weight loss, established complications such as proliferative retinopathy, diabetic kidney disease or a non-healing foot ulcer, and often needs insulin
severity.critical: A1C above 11.0% or a hyperglycemic emergency with dehydration, acidosis or altered mental status, or a life-threatening complication such as myocardial infarction, stroke or sepsis from an infected foot

red_flags.finding: Vomiting, deep rapid breathing or fruity breath
red_flags.meaning: Diabetic ketoacidosis; needs urgent fluids, insulin and electrolyte monitoring

red_flags.finding: Glucose above 600 mg/dL with confusion or focal neurologic deficits
red_flags.meaning: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state; high mortality without prompt treatment

red_flags.finding: Chest pain, pressure or unexplained shortness of breath
red_flags.meaning: Silent myocardial infarction is common in diabetes and may present without classic pain

red_flags.finding: Sudden one-sided weakness, facial droop or trouble speaking
red_flags.meaning: Acute stroke; time-critical evaluation and treatment

red_flags.finding: A foot ulcer with spreading redness, foul drainage, crepitus or black tissue
red_flags.meaning: Deep infection or necrotizing fasciitis; surgical emergency

red_flags.finding: Sudden painless vision loss or new floaters
red_flags.meaning: Vitreous hemorrhage or retinal detachment from proliferative retinopathy

red_flags.finding: Hypotension, tachycardia or altered mental status
red_flags.meaning: Sepsis, hypovolemia or adrenal insufficiency; needs immediate resuscitation

complications.name: Diabetic ketoacidosis
clues: Large urine ketones with low bicarbonate
Often triggered by infection or missed insulin

complications.name: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
clues: Profound dehydration and altered mental status

complications.name: Hypoglycemia
clues: Confusion or seizure with severe lows
Often from insulin or sulfonylureas, missed meals or exercise

complications.name: Diabetic retinopathy
clues: Microaneurysms and dot-blot hemorrhages on dilated exam
Long duration of diabetes and poor control

complications.name: Diabetic kidney disease
clues: Persistent albuminuria on urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio

complications.name: Peripheral neuropathy
clues: Symmetric stocking-distribution numbness, tingling or burning
Loss of vibration sense and ankle reflexes
Loss of protective sensation on monofilament testing

complications.name: Diabetic foot ulcer and infection
clues: Non-healing ulcer at a pressure point
Callus, deformity and dry fissured skin
Diminished pedal pulses or loss of sensation

complications.name: Coronary artery disease and myocardial infarction
clues: May be silent or present with atypical symptoms
ST depression or T-wave changes on ECG

complications.name: Autonomic neuropathy
clues: Gastroparesis with early satiety and vomiting

complications.name: Infections
clues: Candidal infections of skin and genitals

special_populations.differences: Type 2 diabetes in children and teens usually comes with obesity and a strong family history; they may have no symptoms and be found on screening, or present with acanthosis nigricans and high blood pressure. Metformin and lifestyle change are first-line, and the disease progresses faster than in adults.

Symptoms are often blamed on aging; thirst may be blunted, and they may present with confusion, falls, poor wound healing or a hyperglycemic emergency. A1C targets are often relaxed to avoid hypoglycemia, and sulfonylureas and insulin are used cautiously.

High blood sugar first found in pregnancy is usually gestational diabetes; it is often silent and picked up on routine screening, and it raises the risk of later type 2 diabetes. Tight control reduces macrosomia and shoulder dystocia, and insulin is preferred when medication is needed.

Patients with obesity may have insulin resistance and acanthosis nigricans for years before glucose rises; symptoms stay mild and the diagnosis is often made on screening labs. Weight loss of 5 to 10% can improve glucose substantially, and GLP-1 receptor agonists and bariatric surgery are options.
Metformin is avoided when eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 and dose-reduced at 30 to 45; many other agents need dose adjustment, and insulin requirements fall as kidney function declines.
Glucocorticoids and calcineurin inhibitors used for immunosuppression raise glucose; infections are more severe and atypical, and glucose control is harder during treatment.

key_questions.question: Have you been more thirsty than usual?
key_questions.looking_for: Constant, hard-to-satisfy thirst, often worse at night

key_questions.question: How often are you urinating, including at night?
key_questions.looking_for: Frequent urination, especially waking at night to urinate

key_questions.question: How have your energy levels been?
key_questions.looking_for: Persistent tiredness or low energy, often attributed to aging

key_questions.question: Have you lost weight without trying?
How long have these symptoms been going on, and did they come on slowly or suddenly?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over months to years; sudden onset over days suggests type 1 diabetes or ketoacidosis

key_questions.question: Has your vision been blurry or changing?
key_questions.looking_for: Blurred vision that fluctuates with glucose levels

key_questions.question: Any numbness, tingling or burning in your feet or hands?
key_questions.looking_for: Symmetric stocking-distribution sensory symptoms suggesting neuropathy

key_questions.question: Have you had any sores or cuts that are slow to heal?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor wound healing, especially on the feet

key_questions.question: Have you had frequent yeast infections or urinary tract infections?
Any vomiting, deep rapid breathing, fruity-smelling breath or severe abdominal pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Features of diabetic ketoacidosis or a hyperglycemic emergency

key_questions.question: Any chest pain, pressure or unexplained shortness of breath?
key_questions.looking_for: Silent myocardial infarction, which is common in diabetes

key_questions.question: Any sudden weakness on one side, facial droop or trouble speaking?
Do you have high blood pressure, high cholesterol, heart disease or a prior stroke?
key_questions.looking_for: Cardiovascular risk factors and metabolic syndrome

key_questions.question: Have you ever been told your blood sugar was high, or that you had prediabetes or gestational diabetes?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior prediabetes, gestational diabetes or a baby weighing 9 pounds or more

key_questions.question: Do you take any steroids, antipsychotics, thiazide diuretics or transplant medicines?
key_questions.looking_for: Medications that can raise glucose such as prednisone, olanzapine, quetiapine, hydrochlorothiazide or tacrolimus

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have diabetes?
key_questions.looking_for: Type 2 diabetes in a parent or sibling

key_questions.question: How much do you exercise, and what does a typical day of eating look like?
key_questions.looking_for: Sedentary lifestyle, high intake of refined carbohydrates and sugar-sweetened drinks

key_questions.question: Have you had any trouble getting or keeping an erection?
key_questions.looking_for: Erectile dysfunction as a sign of vascular or neuropathic complications

reasoning_points: Gradual onset over months to years of thirst, frequent urination and fatigue in an adult with risk factors
Overweight or obesity with central adiposity, and sometimes acanthosis nigricans
A1C of 6.5% or higher, or fasting plasma glucose of 126 mg/dL or higher, or a random glucose of 200 mg/dL or higher with classic symptoms
An abnormal screening result is confirmed with a repeat test unless the patient has unequivocal symptoms with a glucose of 200 mg/dL or higher
Type 1 diabetes is considered and excluded when the patient is young, lean, or has ketones and acidosis
Complications are assessed at diagnosis, including retinopathy, kidney disease, neuropathy and cardiovascular risk

easy: Middle-aged adult with obesity and a family history of diabetes
Classic thirst, frequent urination and fatigue over months
A1C well above 6.5% with a fasting glucose above 126 mg/dL
medium: No symptoms, diagnosis made on routine screening labs
Older adult whose thirst and fatigue are blamed on aging
Recurrent yeast infections or a non-healing foot sore as the presenting complaint
Mild hyperglycemia with a normal A1C due to anemia or recent transfusion
hard: Young, lean patient who could have type 1 diabetes or monogenic diabetes
Glucose above 600 mg/dL with confusion and profound dehydration suggesting hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
Vomiting and deep rapid breathing suggesting ketoacidosis as the first presentation
Hyperglycemia that appears only after starting prednisone or an atypical antipsychotic
Pregnant patient with silent hyperglycemia found on routine screening
